meta.method: Mechanical passage grouping (lib/prophecy/normalize.ts refKey over the five verbatim source lists; 329 groups) followed by an AI naming pass in 6 batches: one neutral claim per distinct proposition per group, per-entry matchType/confidence/rationale. Claims never span passage groups; cross-passage merging is left to human review. All records load as status=draft for spot-checking.

claims.text: A savior would come to resolve the problem of sin and reconcile humanity to God.
claims.summary: Read as the first messianic promise (the 'protoevangelium'); in context, God's curse on the serpent in Eden.

mappings.rationale: asserts the savior promise and nothing else

claims.text: The messiah would be a human being descended from Eve, the 'seed of the woman'.
claims.summary: 'Seed of the woman' read as the messiah's human descent from Eve; in context the Eden serpent curse.

mappings.rationale: covers only the humanity component (human, not angel)
bundles born-of-a-woman and human-not-angel, jointly this claim

claims.text: The messiah would be born of a virgin, as the 'seed of the woman'.
claims.summary: Two lists gloss 'seed of a woman' as a virgin-birth prediction; in context the Eden serpent curse.

claims.text: The messiah would bruise (crush) Satan's head, defeating him.
claims.summary: The serpent's head-wound read as the messiah's defeat of Satan; the classic protoevangelium reading.

mappings.rationale: asserts the head-bruising and nothing else
bundles defeat of evil with its cost to the messiah

claims.text: The messiah would suffer and die for the benefit of others.
claims.summary: Read into the protoevangelium as the cost of the victory: the promised deliverer suffers and dies for others.

mappings.rationale: asserts vicarious suffering and death directly
bundles the at-his-own-expense element with defeat of evil

claims.text: The messiah would restore what Adam and Eve lost, including eternal life in a perfect world.
claims.summary: A theological extrapolation from Genesis 3: the promised deliverer reverses the losses of Eden.

mappings.rationale: list's own restoration extrapolation, asserted as a single proposition

claims.text: The messiah's heel would be bruised in his conflict with the serpent.
claims.summary: The heel-bruise of Gen 3:15 read as the messiah's wounding; the list ties it to crucifixion nails.

mappings.rationale: entry's own gloss ties the heel bruise to the nails of the cross

claims.text: The messiah would be merciful in character.
claims.summary: Exod 33:19 is God proclaiming his own goodness to Moses; two lists read it as the messiah's merciful character.

mappings.rationale: character gloss on a theophany text; single proposition

claims.text: The messiah would give his lifeblood for others.
claims.summary: Lev 17:11's rule that the life of the flesh is in the blood, read as prefiguring the messiah giving his lifeblood.

mappings.rationale: sacrificial-blood principle applied to the messiah's ransom sayings

claims.text: The messiah's blood would make atonement for sin.
claims.summary: Lev 17:11's atonement-by-blood principle read as prefiguring the messiah's atoning blood.

claims.text: The messiah would bear a curse by being hanged on a tree.
claims.summary: Deut 21:23's rule that a hanged criminal is cursed, read via Galatians 3 as pointing to the crucifixion.

mappings.rationale: legal rule applied to the messiah via Gal 3:13

claims.text: The messiah would be God's anointed king.
claims.summary: From Hannah's song; its closing line about strength for 'his anointed' king is read by the lists as the messiah.

mappings.rationale: same proposition, near-verbatim of the verse

claims.text: God would never take his steadfast love away from the messiah.
claims.summary: From Nathan's Davidic-covenant oracle about David's successor; read as spoken of the messiah.

mappings.rationale: reads the covenant promise to David's heir as messianic

claims.text: The messiah would reign on David's throne forever.
claims.summary: The Davidic covenant as retold in Chronicles, read as promising the messiah's unending reign.

claims.text: The messiah would be the mediator between God and humanity.
claims.summary: Job's wish for an arbiter between himself and God, read by one list as pointing to a messianic mediator.

mappings.rationale: asserts the mediator role and nothing else

claims.text: The messiah would have power over death.
claims.summary: Job's 'I know that my redeemer lives', read as a messianic statement of mastery over death.

mappings.rationale: asserts power over death; fulfillments cited are the raising miracles

claims.text: The messiah would bear the title 'Anointed' as God's anointed one.
claims.summary: Psalm 2's royal enthronement scene; 'his anointed' read as the messianic title Christ.

mappings.rationale: asserts ownership of the title Anointed/Christ

claims.text: The messiah would be praised out of the mouths of children.
claims.summary: Psalm 8's praise 'from the mouths of babes', linked by the lists to Jesus' temple quotation of the verse.

claims.text: The messiah would rise from death.
claims.summary: The psalmist's hope of waking satisfied in God's likeness, read by two lists as predicting resurrection.

mappings.rationale: asserts 'the resurrection predicted' and nothing else

claims.text: The messiah would be mocked and insulted by onlookers who sneer and shake their heads.
claims.summary: Psalm 22's lament imagery of sneering, head-shaking onlookers, read as the mockery of the messiah.

mappings.rationale: quotes the verse's lip-and-head imagery; same proposition

claims.text: The messiah would suffer severe thirst and dehydration during his suffering.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:14-15's 'poured out like water… tongue sticks to my jaws', read as the messiah's dying thirst.

claims.text: The messiah would die of a broken (ruptured) heart.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:14's melted-wax heart read by one list as a literal ruptured heart at death.

mappings.rationale: reads 'my heart is like wax' as a physiological cause of death

claims.text: The messiah's blood would be poured out when his side was pierced.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:14's 'poured out like water' read as blood pouring from a pierced side.

mappings.rationale: asserts the pierced-side blood reading specifically

claims.text: The messiah would suffer extreme physical agony at his execution.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:14-15 read broadly as the messiah's physical agony at his execution.

claims.text: God would hear and respond to the messiah's cry for help.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:24: God does not hide from the afflicted one's cry; read as God answering the messiah.

mappings.rationale: asserts the answered-cry proposition; fulfillment cited is the resurrection

claims.text: The messiah's dying declaration would be that the work was finished.
claims.summary: Psalm 22:31's closing 'he has done it', linked by the lists to the last words 'It is finished'.

claims.text: The messiah's friends and acquaintances would abandon him and flee.
claims.summary: Psalm 31:11: the psalmist shunned by acquaintances; read as the messiah's followers deserting him.

mappings.rationale: worded as foreshadowing of rejection; cites the disciples' flight

claims.text: The messiah would go about doing good.
claims.summary: Psalm 38:20: David pursued for following what is good; read as describing the messiah's benevolent conduct.

mappings.rationale: brief character gloss; single clear proposition

claims.text: The messiah would serve as the final sacrifice, permanently atoning for sin.
claims.summary: Psalm 40:6-8's sacrifice-not-desired theme read (via Hebrews 10) as the messiah replacing the sacrificial system.

mappings.rationale: bundles obedience to God's will with the ultimate-sacrifice proposition

claims.text: The messiah would delight in doing God's will.
claims.summary: Psalm 40:8 'I delight to do your will' read as the messiah's devotion to the Father's will.

mappings.rationale: bundles obedience/delight with the ultimate-sacrifice proposition

claims.text: The messiah's betrayer would die unrepentant.
claims.summary: Psalm 55's curse on a treacherous companion, read as predicting the fate of the messiah's betrayer.

claims.text: The messiah would be consumed with zeal for God's house.
claims.summary: Psalm 69:9a 'zeal for your house consumes me', applied to the messiah via the temple-cleansing episode.

claims.text: The messiah would bear the reproaches of those who reproach God.
claims.summary: Psalm 69:9b: reproaches aimed at God fall on the psalmist; read as spoken by the messiah.

mappings.rationale: asserts the reproach-bearing half of the verse specifically

claims.text: The messiah's reign and influence would extend across the whole world.
claims.summary: Psalm 72, a royal psalm of universal dominion, read as the messiah's worldwide impact.

mappings.rationale: fulfillment cited is the historical spread of Christianity

claims.text: The messiah, like a grain of wheat falling into the ground, would die to produce abundance.
claims.summary: Psalm 72:16's abundant-grain image linked by the lists to the seed-must-die saying of John 12:24.

mappings.rationale: connects an agricultural abundance image to the John 12 saying

claims.text: The messiah would endure deep suffering and public reproach.
claims.summary: Psalm 88, the bleakest individual lament in the Psalter, read whole by one list as the messiah's suffering.

mappings.rationale: maps an entire lament psalm to the passion as one suffering proposition

claims.text: God's covenant with David, carrying the promise of the messiah, would endure forever.
claims.summary: Psalm 89 recites the Davidic covenant; read as guaranteeing the messianic promise forever.

claims.text: The messiah would be exalted above all earthly kings.
claims.summary: Psalm 89:27b: the Davidic king as 'highest of the kings of the earth', read of the messiah.

claims.text: The messiah would be God's firstborn.
claims.summary: Psalm 89:27a 'I will make him my firstborn', read as a messianic title.

mappings.rationale: asserts the firstborn title alone, distinct from the kings claim

claims.text: The messiah would suffer overwhelming affliction and reproach.
claims.summary: Psalm 102:1-11, an afflicted man's lament, read whole as the messiah's suffering and reproach.

mappings.rationale: whole-lament reading applied to the passion as one proposition

claims.text: The messiah would be compassionate and gracious in character.
claims.summary: Psalm 112:4 describes the upright man as gracious and compassionate; read as the messiah's character.

claims.text: The messiah would be presented to Israel with the blessing 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD'.
claims.summary: Psalm 118:26's pilgrim blessing, read as the crowd's greeting of the messiah at his arrival.

claims.text: The messiah would come while the Temple in Jerusalem was still standing.
claims.summary: Reads Psalm 118's procession 'from the house of the LORD' as dating the messiah's arrival to the temple era.

mappings.rationale: same timing proposition, letter-split from the presentation entry

claims.text: The messiah's parables would fall on uncomprehending ears.
claims.summary: Isa 6:9-10, Isaiah's commission to a dull-hearted people, applied to the reception of the parables.

claims.text: The people would remain blind to the messiah and deaf to his words.
claims.summary: Isa 6:9-12's blindness-and-deafness theme applied to the wider rejection of the messiah's message.

mappings.rationale: general-rejection proposition, split by the list from its parables entry

claims.text: The messiah would reign on David's throne in a government and peace without end.
claims.summary: Isa 9:7 on the endless increase of the Davidic government and peace, read as the messiah's reign.

mappings.rationale: everlasting-kingdom wording asserts the whole claim

claims.text: The messiah would be just and righteous.
claims.summary: Isa 9:7's justice-and-righteousness language read as the messiah's personal character.

mappings.rationale: bundles just-and-righteous with the eternity claim

claims.text: The Gentiles (the nations) would seek the messiah.

mappings.rationale: bundles worldwide impact with the humble-and-gentle claim

claims.text: The messiah would open the eyes of the blind.
claims.summary: Isa 42:7, the Servant's commission to open blind eyes, read as the messiah's healings of the blind.

claims.text: The messiah would be the judge before whom every knee bows.
claims.summary: Isa 45:23 'to me every knee shall bow', transferred by the lists to the messiah as universal judge.

claims.text: The messiah would be heard by peoples throughout the world.

mappings.rationale: 'called from the womb' with an added humanity gloss

claims.text: The messiah would be struck on the face and cheeks.
claims.summary: Isa 50:6's cheeks given 'to those who pluck the beard', read as blows to the messiah's face.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry for the spitting clause

claims.text: The messiah would willingly submit to abuse without resisting.
claims.summary: Isa 50:6's unresisting Servant read as the messiah's willing submission to mistreatment.

mappings.rationale: asserts the willing-submission proposition, distinct from the specific abuses

claims.text: The messiah would be shamed, insulted, and dishonored.
claims.summary: Isa 50:6's 'shame and spitting' read as the messiah's public dishonor.

mappings.rationale: asserts the shaming proposition, split by the list from spitting and beating

claims.text: The messiah would remain silent before his accusers.
claims.summary: Isa 53:7 (Suffering Servant song of Isa 52-53): a lamb silent before its shearers; read as silence at trial.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the silence clause

claims.text: The messiah would be oppressed, afflicted, and persecuted.
claims.summary: Isa 53:7a 'oppressed and afflicted' (Suffering Servant song), read as the messiah's persecution.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the oppression clause
'persecuted' wording; same proposition and cited fulfillment

claims.text: The messiah would be led like a sacrificial lamb to the slaughter.
claims.summary: Isa 53:7's lamb-to-slaughter image (Suffering Servant song), read as the messiah as sacrificial lamb.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the lamb clause

claims.text: The messiah would go cooperatively, without resistance, to his death.
claims.summary: Isa 53:7's unprotesting Servant read as the messiah's cooperation on the way to his death.

mappings.rationale: asserts cooperation en route to death, distinct from the same list's silence entry

claims.text: The messiah would be raised from death by God.
claims.summary: Isa 55:3's 'sure mercies of David' read, following Acts 13:34, as a resurrection promise.

mappings.rationale: resurrection reading depends entirely on the Acts 13 use of the verse

claims.text: God would glorify the messiah.
claims.summary: Isa 55:5: God glorifies the Davidic figure addressed; read of the messiah via Acts 3:13.

mappings.rationale: asserts the glorification proposition; single terse entry

claims.text: The messiah would come to provide salvation.
claims.summary: Isa 59:15-16: no intercessor found, so God's own arm brings salvation; read as the messiah's advent.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the salvation-provision clause

claims.text: The messiah would intercede between God and humanity.
claims.summary: Isa 59:16's missing intercessor read as the messiah filling the intercessor role.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the intercessor clause

claims.text: The Spirit of God would rest upon the messiah.
claims.summary: Isa 61:1a: the Spirit of the Lord GOD upon the anointed herald; read of the messiah.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry for the Spirit clause

umbrella entry asserting the whole Isa 61 ministry program

mappings.rationale: list's own two-phase schema, keyed to where Jesus stopped reading in Luke 4

claims.text: The messiah would defeat death itself.
claims.summary: Hosea 13:14's ransom-from-Sheol line read, via 1 Cor 15:55, as the messiah's victory over death.

claims.text: A future ruler of Israel would be born in Bethlehem.

claims.text: The house of David would survive existential threats until the messiah was born.
claims.summary: One list reads Micah 5's Assyrian-crisis context as a promise the dynasty survives until the birth.

claims.text: The messiah would be the stone that God himself sets.
claims.summary: Zech 3:9's engraved stone set before Joshua the high priest, read as a symbol of the messiah.

mappings.rationale: asserts the stone symbol; reading rests on the foundation-stone metaphor of 1 Cor 3

claims.text: The messiah would be presented to Jerusalem riding on a donkey.
claims.summary: Zech 9:9: Zion's king comes lowly, riding on a donkey; read as the messiah's entry into Jerusalem.

mappings.rationale: asserts the donkey-riding entry and nothing else

claims.text: At the messiah's coming, Israel would be under unfit leaders.
claims.summary: Zech 11's doomed-flock allegory of worthless shepherds, applied to Israel's leadership at the time.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the unfit-leaders proposition

claims.text: Israel's rejection of the messiah would cause God to withdraw his protection.
claims.summary: Zech 11:6: God will no longer pity the land's inhabitants; read as protection withdrawn after rejection.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the withdrawn-protection proposition

claims.text: The messiah would be rejected in favor of another king.
claims.summary: Zech 11's rejected-shepherd narrative read as Israel preferring another king over the messiah.

mappings.rationale: letter-split entry asserting the rejected-for-another-king proposition

claims.text: The messiah would be God's shepherd.
claims.summary: Zech 13:7's 'my shepherd' read as the messiah in the role of God's shepherd.

claims.summary: Zech 13:7's sword awakening against the shepherd, read as the messiah's violent death.

mappings.rationale: 'a violent death' gloss on the sword against the shepherd

claims.text: When the shepherd was struck, his flock would be scattered.
claims.summary: Zech 13:7b 'strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered', read of the messiah's followers.

mappings.rationale: reads the scattering as Israel's, though the cited fulfillment is the disciples' flight

claims.summary: The sword commanded by God in Zech 13:7 read as God willing the messiah's death for mankind.

claims.text: The messiah would be both God and man.
claims.summary: Zech 13:7's 'the man who is my fellow' read as asserting the messiah's deity and humanity.

claims.summary: Enoch 'walked with God and was not'; the lists read his removal as an illustration of a bodily ascension to heaven.

claims.summary: The promise of Isaac to aged Sarah; the list reads the miracle-birth pattern as prefiguring Jesus' birth.

mappings.rationale: wording itself frames it as a foreshadowing parallel

claims.text: The near-sacrifice of Isaac would foreshadow the sacrificial death of the messiah.
claims.summary: The Akedah (binding of Isaac); the list reads the episode as a type of Jesus' sacrifice.

claims.text: The messiah would be a descendant of Abraham.

bundles Isaac-line descent with the all-nations blessing

claims.summary: The 'seed of Abraham' blessing formula; lists read the singular 'seed' as the messiah blessing all nations.

mappings.rationale: bundles the blessing claim with Isaac-line descent
same wording as the 324 list's entry 12

claims.text: The messiah would be an unblemished sacrificial lamb, as prefigured by the Passover lamb.
claims.summary: The Passover regulation requiring a flawless lamb; lists read it as a type of Christ's sacrifice via 1 Peter 1:19.

mappings.rationale: same wording as the 324 list's entry 20

claims.text: The messiah would be exalted as God's salvation, identified with the name Yeshua.
claims.summary: A line of the Song of the Sea ('the LORD... is become my salvation'); lists read 'salvation' (yeshuah) as naming the messiah.

mappings.rationale: same wording as the 324 list's entry 24

claims.text: The messiah's sacrifice would be a pleasing aroma to God, as prefigured by the burnt offering.
claims.summary: Burnt-offering regulations; the list draws an offering parallel to Christ's self-offering via Ephesians 5:2.

claims.text: The Day of Atonement sin offering would prefigure the messiah's once-for-all sacrificial death.
claims.summary: Yom Kippur ritual instructions; the lists themselves label this a prefiguration, following Hebrews 9.

mappings.rationale: same wording as the 324 list's entry 29

claims.text: The bronze serpent lifted on a pole would prefigure the messiah's being lifted up.
claims.summary: The bronze-serpent episode in the wilderness; lists read it as a type of the crucifixion via John 3:14.

mappings.rationale: same wording as the 324 list's entry 35

claims.summary: Close of the 'prophet like Moses' passage; the list applies the warning about non-listeners to the messiah.

claims.text: Those who refuse to listen to the promised prophet would be held to account by God.
claims.summary: The same verse's sanction clause ('I will require it of him'), read messianically by the lists.

mappings.rationale: 'must bear his sin' is the accountability clause
same wording as the 324 list's entry 40
